transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-29
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tomás (Redwood SE), Priya, Evan, Sara, Jon (Amberfield)

Summary: quick intro, network constraints (regions + egress), private endpoints vs peering, security controls (KMS, audit), pilot plan and IP planning.

Topics: 1) Regions and data residency 2) VPC peering vs PrivateLink 3) CIDR/IP planning and Transit Gateway concerns 4) Firewall and egress rules 5) Pilot next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: alright hi everyone thanks for taking the time today, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the account lead, and with me is Tomás our solutions engineer. nice to meet you all.
[00:10] Priya Rao: hey thanks Maya, Priya here, i'll kick things off from infra side. couple constraints up front: we are a financial org, low tolerance for plaintext egress, we need private network only, and we have strict region gating—no model data can leave us-east-1 or eu-west-1 depending on the product.
[00:28] Tomás Alvarez: got it, thanks Priya. quick clarifying q: are you evaluating Hosted with VPC onramp or do you plan fully Private (VPC-only) deployment?
[00:36] Evan Mills: product wants private deployment — a private control plane if possible. we also are evaluating a dedicated capacity option but initial requirement is private VPC peering or private endpoints into redwood.
[00:46] Sara Nguyen: and to be clear, our compliance team needs to see KMS integration, per-request audit logs, and we--- we may want customer-managed keys.
[00:55] Maya Chen: great. one note: Redwood Private supports a customer-managed KMS flow and we can ship audit logs to your S3/Cloudwatch logs. we'll include the SOC2 docs in the security pack.
[01:05] Jon Park: timeline? we want a pilot in staging in ~2 weeks if possible, production by end of Q1.
[01:12] Tomás Alvarez: that's aggressive, doable if network handoff and IP space are ready. typical blockers i see: CIDR overlap, transit gateway limits, egress NAT/inspection, and region gating for where our private endpoints can sit.
[01:25] Priya Rao: we use AWS primarily (us-east-1 and eu-west-1). we have existing transit gateway for inter-VPC traffic, but security prefers private endpoints rather than classic peering because peering means route-table propagation and we want more explicit control.
[01:40] Maya Chen: noted. a couple clarifying items — when you say private endpoint, do you mean AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint) into Redwood's private service, or do you want an L3 VPC peering adjacency to our private worker VPC?
[01:52] Evan Mills: prefer PrivateLink if it avoids cross-account route table changes. but need to validate performance; we do talk latency-sensitive features.
[02:00] Tomás Alvarez: PrivateLink semantics: it goes over ENIs in your VPC and is more firewall-friendly, but throughput and connection scaling are factors. we can provide benchmarking numbers, and for high throughput we sometimes recommend dedicated peering with dedicated capacity where we can pin bandwidth.
[02:16] Sara Nguyen: throughput numbers would be great. also want to understand IP ranges you will advertise, and whether we need NAT for egress to your control plane. we cannot expose any public internet egress from model data plane.
[02:29] Tomás Alvarez: we can give you a minimal set of IP blocks for the private endpoint or peering, and we support an entirely private dataplane. our private control plane can either be customer-managed in your VPC or hosted with PrivateLink tunnel back — depends on the package.
[02:44] Priya Rao: explain the customer-managed control plane option — do you install something, or is it just network-level?
[02:49] Maya Chen: customer-managed means we deploy the control plane components in a dedicated account or in your VPC; for on-prem or air gap customers we provide an appliance/helm chart. for most customers we do a VPC-hosted control plane that talks to the data plane over private endpoints.
[03:03] Priya Rao: okay. can you do a diagram?
[03:06] Maya Chen: yes we'll attach a network diagram and the peering vs PrivateLink pros/cons doc.
[03:11] [00:03:12] Evan Mills: another point — our CIDR hygiene is pretty tight. current address space: 10.0.0.0/16 for prod, 10.1.0.0/16 for staging. we have small on-prem NATs into cloud. we need to avoid overlaps.
[03:24] Tomás Alvarez: suggested pattern: provision a /22 for the managed endpoints, non-overlapping with yours, and avoid using the 100.64/10 space if you have carrier NAT. we'll draft a recommended IP plan.
[03:36] Sara Nguyen: firewall: our IDS/IPS needs to inspect traffic to redwood for egress rules. is there TLS termination on your side? do you support mTLS?
[03:45] Maya Chen: we support TLS1.2/1.3 and mTLS for PrivateLink and VPC peering connections; for customer-managed control plane we can enforce mutual TLS with certs bound to KMS-managed keys.
[03:57] Jon Park: region gating — we have separate product lines, some must stay eu-west-1, some must be us-east-1. can Redwood run model instances in both regions and direct traffic accordingly?
[04:08] Tomás Alvarez: yes we support multi-region deployments. routing policies can be set at the request layer — your app can hit the region-specific endpoint. for private endpoints we'd create endpoints in both regions. note: cross-region peering adds complexity — better to keep per-region private endpoints.
[04:23] Priya Rao: is there any data egress between regions from Redwood backend? we need to ensure no cross-region replica of logs or model cache.
[04:31] Maya Chen: by default we keep caches local to region; we can disable cross-region replication of logs and ensure log storage is region-bound. we'll include that in the security doc.
[04:41] [00:04:45] Evan Mills: ok can we talk about perf — if we do PrivateLink in us-east-1, what kind of latency to expect for 512 token responses?
[04:50] Tomás Alvarez: our baseline median p50 for 512 tokens on dedicated capacity in us-east is ~120-180ms downstream per token? (note: vocalizing, numbers approximate). with PrivateLink overlay add maybe 10-30ms, depends on ENI and cross-account hops. we will run a benchmark from your staging to give real numbers.
[05:07] Sara Nguyen: and cost — we need to vet the cost of PrivateLink ENIs and data processing fees as compared to peering traffic across transit gateway.
[05:15] Maya Chen: yes we can provide cost models. PrivateLink has per-GB data charge plus ENI/hour; peering is free but transit gateway carries per-hour/GB costs — tradeoff depends on traffic profile. Redwood Optimize can help model that based on request shaping.
[05:30] Priya Rao: about credentials: will tokens be exchanged across PrivateLink or do you use SRV side keys? where are keys stored?
[05:36] Tomás Alvarez: authentication is via per-tenant API keys plus mutual TLS if desired. keys can be rotated; for customer-managed KMS we integrate with your KMS for envelope encryption.
[05:45] [00:05:50] Priya Rao: our security wants end-to-end proof — can you provide an architecture diagram showing KMS flow and where logs land?
[05:54] Maya Chen: yes, included in security pack.
[05:57] Jon Park: procurement and timeline — if we proceed with a pilot, do you have an onboarding runbook?
[06:03] Maya Chen: absolutely, the runbook covers peering setup, firewall rules, sample allowlist CIDRs, and a test harness for latency/throughput. it also includes rollback steps. we'll send that with the pack.
[06:11] Evan Mills: one specific question: our staging subnet is behind a NAT that performs egress inspection—will that break the PrivateLink connection?
[06:18] Tomás Alvarez: PrivateLink is initiated from your side and is TCP over ENIs — NAT should be fine for outbound control traffic; for streaming token connections if you have stateful inspection we recommend pinning flows or allowing the ENI CIDRs. we'll give the full list of ports (443 + range for streaming).
[06:34] Sara Nguyen: about cert provisioning — do we need to manage certs or can Redwood generate and rotate for us?
[06:39] Maya Chen: we can support both; for strict compliance customers often prefer to provision certs via their internal PKI; Redwood can also rotate on your behalf and provide audit trails.
[06:49] [00:06:55] Priya Rao: any gotchas with cross-account PrivateLink? we have strict SCPs in org that limit CreateNetworkInterface in shared accounts.
[07:02] Tomás Alvarez: yes that can block endpoint creation; two workarounds: 1) we deploy a service consumer VPC in a delegated account and you approve the endpoint via your console; or 2) use VPC peering initiated by the customer and we provide the target peer. we'll document both paths.
[07:16] Evan Mills: do you support transit gateway attachments? we want to avoid many peering pairs.
[07:21] Tomás Alvarez: we support TGW attachments; Redwood-managed VPCs can attach to your TGW. note TGW has route limit considerations; we'll include recommended route table sizing.
[07:33] [00:07:34] Jon Park: audit & retention — what retention windows for logs? we need minimum 7 years for some records.
[07:42] Maya Chen: we ship logs to your controlled bucket and retention is set by you; Redwood keeps an additional short-term copy for ops (configurable, we can opt-out).
[07:51] Sara Nguyen: can we get a demo of the control plane UI in a follow-up?
[07:55] Maya Chen: yes, we'll schedule product demo with our console team.
[07:58] Priya Rao: ok next steps recap?
[08:00] Maya Chen: recap: we'll send security pack, network diagram, IP plan draft, and perf baseline action. you'll share VPC diagram and constrained regions. aim to schedule pilot kickoff 2/12.
[08:12] Evan Mills: noted. any blockers from Redwood SLA or compliance?
[08:16] Maya Chen: nothing blocking; our enterprise team will work with you on contract terms for dedicated/private setups.
[08:22] Jon Park: great, thank you all.
[08:24] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[08:30] [00:08:30] End of meeting
